title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits
authors: Michael Poppel, David Bucher, Maximilian Zorn, Markus Baumann, Sebastian Wölckert, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, Philipp Altmann, Jonas Stein
abstract: Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.
summary: This paper rigorously compares single-qubit versus multi-qubit quantum circuits designed to represent the same function. It proves that while they are equally expressive, the single-qubit serial structure suffers from 'phase-locking,' which geometrically constrains its parameter movement. This constraint leads to significantly poorer convergence during first-order training compared to multi-qubit controls.
main_problem: The paper compares the training difficulty of single-qubit versus multi-qubit variational quantum circuits (VQCs) that are structurally different but functionally equivalent (same spectrum). It investigates whether the structural trade-off between width and depth impacts optimization convergence.
main_result: The exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training; the single-qubit serial circuit exhibits 'phase-locking' that severely limits its tangent directions compared to multi-qubit controls, leading to poorer optimization performance.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis of the Jacobian structure (comparing tangent directions) alongside extensive numerical benchmarking using multiple optimization algorithms (Adam, LM, GD) on various target functions.
model_or_system: The model involves Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) using angle encoding to implement truncated Fourier series. The comparison is between serial (single-qubit) and multi-qubit (ancilla/parallel) circuit architectures.
key_observables: Convergence rate (runs out of 100 reaching optimum), held-out error ratio, and the dimension of the tangent space ($	ext{dim T}$).
important_parameters: Encoding budget ($E$), number of qubits ($N$), and optimization algorithm (Adam, LM, GD).
main_assumptions: The comparison focuses on optimization difficulty, not a loss of expressivity, and assumes the cost is due to optimization geometry rather than vanishing gradients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate chain lengths for different circuit types and demonstrate the phase-locking mechanism (one complex direction for $N=1$). Tables summarize convergence rates and error ratios across various targets and optimizers.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the functional equivalence of the circuits (same spectrum) and then dives into the theoretical analysis of the Jacobian structure, highlighting the constraint imposed by phase-locking in the serial case. This is followed by extensive numerical results comparing optimization performance across different real-world and synthetic targets.
why_interesting: The findings provide concrete evidence that the geometric structure of the quantum circuit (depth vs. width) imposes measurable, non-trivial constraints on the optimization landscape, which is crucial for designing efficient quantum machine learning models.
